claim: Locomotion is controlled by spinal circuits that interact with supraspinal drives and sensory feedback from the limbs.
source: Locomotion is controlled by spinal circuits that interact with supraspinal drives and sensory feedback from the limbs.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding about locomotor control, supported by the citations that follow in the manuscript.

claim: Sensorimotor interactions are disrupted following spinal cord injury.
source: These sensorimotor interactions are disrupted following spinal cord injury.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge about the effects of spinal cord injury.

claim: The thoracic lateral hemisection represents an experimental model of an incomplete spinal cord injury where connections between the brain and spinal cord are abolished on one side of the cord.
source: The thoracic lateral hemisection represents an experimental model of an incomplete spinal cord injury, where connections between the brain and spinal cord are abolished on one side of the cord.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the hemisection model based on established knowledge of the procedure.

claim: The computational model used in this study was recently published in eLife (Rybak et al., 2024).
source: To investigate the effects of such an injury on the operation of the spinal locomotor network, we used our computational model of cat locomotion recently published in eLife (Rybak et al., 2024)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication.

claim: Following hemisection, the contralesional ('intact', left) side of the spinal network is mostly controlled by supraspinal drives.
source: Based on our model, we hypothesized that following hemisection the contralesional ('intact', left) side of the spinal network is mostly controlled by supraspinal drives
evidence: This is a hypothesis derived from the computational model presented in the study.

claim: Following hemisection, the ipsilesional ('hemisected', right) side of the spinal network is mostly controlled by somatosensory feedback.
source: whereas the ipsilesional ('hemisected', right) side is mostly controlled by somatosensory feedback.
evidence: This is a hypothesis derived from the computational model presented in the study.

claim: Experimental results confirmed many effects of hemisection on cat locomotion predicted by simulations.
source: Our experimental results confirmed many effects of hemisection on cat locomotion predicted by our simulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with model predictions presented throughout the Results section.

claim: Having the ipsilesional hindlimb step on the slow belt, but not the fast belt, during split-belt locomotion substantially reduces the effects of lateral hemisection.
source: We show that having the ipsilesional hindlimb step on the slow belt, but not the fast belt, during split-belt locomotion substantially reduces the effects of lateral hemisection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental and simulation data comparing Left slow/Right fast vs. Left fast/Right slow conditions.

claim: Somatosensory feedback plays a major role in the control of locomotion at lower speeds.
source: It has been hypothesized that somatosensory feedback plays a major role in the control of locomotion at lower speeds, and that this role decreases as speed increases (Full and Koditschek, 1999; Holmes et al., 2006; Ijspeert and Daley, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The role of somatosensory feedback in locomotion control decreases as speed increases.
source: It has been hypothesized that somatosensory feedback plays a major role in the control of locomotion at lower speeds, and that this role decreases as speed increases (Full and Koditschek, 1999; Holmes et al., 2006; Ijspeert and Daley, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In humans, most spinal cord injuries are not complete and some pathways that communicate between the brain and spinal cord remain intact.
source: In humans, most SCIs are not complete and some pathways that communicate between the brain and spinal cord remain intact (Harkema et al., 2011; Angeli et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on human spinal cord injuries.

claim: A lateral hemisection reproduces features of the Brown-Séquard syndrome observed in humans.
source: A lateral hemisection, which reproduces features of the Brown-Séquard syndrome observed in humans, abolishes all spinal pathways on one side of the cord (Shams et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A lateral hemisection abolishes all spinal pathways on one side of the cord.
source: A lateral hemisection, which reproduces features of the Brown-Séquard syndrome observed in humans, abolishes all spinal pathways on one side of the cord (Shams et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the hemisection procedure supported by citation.

claim: A lateral hemisection effectively cuts off bidirectional communication between the brain and spinal cord on one side.
source: This effectively cuts off bidirectional communication between the brain and spinal cord on one side.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the hemisection procedure based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: The main feature of locomotion after lateral hemisection is that the locomotor pattern becomes asymmetric with different stance and swing phase durations for the contralesional and ipsilesional hindlimbs.
source: The main feature is that the locomotor pattern becomes asymmetric with different stance and swing phase durations for the contralesional and ipsilesional hindlimbs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies on hemisection effects.

claim: Changes in sensorimotor interactions following a lateral hemisection and their impact on the control of phase durations/transitions remain poorly understood.
source: However, changes in sensorimotor interactions following a lateral hemisection and other incomplete SCIs, as well as their impact on the control of phase durations/transitions, remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, identifying a gap.

claim: A computational model of the neural control of cat hindlimb locomotion was previously built using experimental data from intact cats and cats with complete thoracic SCI.
source: Using experimental data obtained during treadmill locomotion from intact cats and cats with a complete thoracic SCI (i.e. ,spinal transection), we previously built a computational model of the neural control of cat hindlimb locomotion (Rybak et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the previous publication.

claim: Spinal circuits can operate in different regimes depending on the speed of locomotion and available inputs from supraspinal structures and somatosensory feedback.
source: Based on that study, we proposed that spinal circuits can operate in different regimes depending on the speed of locomotion and available inputs from supraspinal structures and somatosensory feedback.
evidence: This is a proposal based on previous modeling work cited in the manuscript.

claim: In the intact condition, spinal circuits operated in a state-machine regime at slow speeds before transitioning to a flexor-driven regime and then to a classical half-center regime at higher speeds.
source: Specifically, in the intact condition, spinal circuits operated in a state-machine regime (an external signal is necessary for the extension-to-flexion transitions) at slow speeds before transitioning to a flexor-driven regime (locomotor activity is defined by the intrinsic oscillations of the flexor half-center) and then to a classical half-center regime (the oscillations require mutual inhibition of both half-centers) at higher speeds.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from the previous modeling study.

claim: In spinal-transected cats, spinal circuits operated exclusively in a state-machine regime, requiring sensory feedback from the limbs to regulate flexor and extensor phase durations across speeds.
source: In spinal-transected cats, however, spinal circuits operated exclusively in a state-machine regime, requiring sensory feedback from the limbs to regulate flexor and extensor phase durations across speeds.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from the previous modeling study.

claim: The model includes two rhythm generators (RGs), each consisting of two conditional bursters representing flexor (F) and extensor (E) half-centers that inhibit each other through inhibitory neurons.
source: Briefly, the spinal circuitry in the model includes two rhythm generators (RGs), each consisting of two conditional bursters, representing flexor (F) and extensor (E) half-centers, respectively, inhibiting each other through inhibitory neurons, InF and InE.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The left and right RGs interact via a series of commissural interneuronal (CIN) pathways mediated by different sets of genetically identified commissural and ipsilaterally projecting interneurons.
source: The left and right RGs interact via a series of commissural interneuronal (CIN) pathways mediated by different sets of genetically identified commissural (V0D, V0V, and V3) and ipsilaterally projecting (V2a) interneurons and some hypothetical inhibitory interneurons (Ini).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The organization of RG interactions was directly drawn from earlier models based on molecular/genetic studies in mice.
source: The organization of these interactions was directly drawn from our earlier models (Rybak et al., 2015; Shevtsova et al., 2015; Danner et al., 2017; Danner et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022; Shevtsova et al., 2022) and was based on the results of previous molecular/genetic studies in mice or proposed to explain and reproduce different aspects of the neural control of locomotion in these studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous modeling and experimental studies.

claim: Each RG can operate in one of three regimes: state-machine, flexor-driven, and classical half-center regimes.
source: As described in detail in our previous paper (Rybak et al., 2024), each RG can operate in one of three regimes: state-machine, flexor-driven, and classical half-center regimes.
evidence: This is a description of model behavior based on the previous publication.

claim: The non-oscillatory state-machine regime requires an external input (e.g., feedback signal) to switch from extension to flexion.
source: Specifically, the non-oscillatory state-machine regime requires an external input (e.g., feedback signal) to switch from extension to flexion.
evidence: This is a description of model behavior based on the previous publication.

claim: In the flexion-driven regime, the RG oscillations are defined by intrinsic bursting properties of the F half-center.
source: In the flexion-driven regime, the RG oscillations are defined by intrinsic bursting properties of the F half-center
evidence: This is a description of model behavior based on the previous publication.

claim: In the classical half-center regime, both half-centers and their mutual inhibition are critically involved in RG oscillations.
source: whereas in the classical half-center regime both half-centers and their mutual inhibition are critically involved in RG oscillations.
evidence: This is a description of model behavior based on the previous publication.

claim: The SF-E1 feedback represents sensory feedback from spindle afferents of hip flexor muscles, whose activity increases when these muscles are stretched during stance.
source: The SF-E1 feedback represents sensory feedback from spindle afferents of hip flexor muscles, whose activity increases when these muscles are stretched when the hip extends during stance (Grillner and Rossignol, 1978; Kriellaars et al., 1994; Pearson, 2004; Pearson, 2008; Klishko et al., 2021; Frigon et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the model component based on cited physiological knowledge.

claim: SF-E1 feedback promotes the extensor-flexor phase transition via excitatory input to the ipsilateral F half-center and inhibitory input to the contralateral F half-center.
source: This feedback promotes the extensor-flexor phase transition via excitatory input to the ipsilateral F half-center and inhibitory input to the contralateral F half-center and increases with increasing treadmill speed.
evidence: This is a description of model behavior based on the model architecture.

claim: SF-E1 feedback increases with increasing treadmill speed.
source: This feedback promotes the extensor-flexor phase transition via excitatory input to the ipsilateral F half-center and inhibitory input to the contralateral F half-center and increases with increasing treadmill speed.
evidence: This is a description of model behavior based on the model architecture.

claim: The SF-E2 feedback simulates the involvement of force-dependent group Ib afferent excitatory feedback from limb extensor muscles to the ipsilateral E half-center, reinforcing extensor activity and weight support during stance.
source: The SF-E2 feedback simulates in a simplified form the involvement of force-dependent group Ib afferent excitatory feedback from limb extensor muscles to the ipsilateral E half-center, reinforcing extensor activity and weight support during stance (Duysens and Pearson, 1980; Pearson and Collins, 1993; Gossard et al., 1994; Frigon et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the model component based on cited physiological knowledge.

claim: In the spinal-transected model, locomotion is entirely defined by sensory feedback from the hindlimbs, operating in a state-machine regime.
source: In the spinal-transected model (lacking supraspinal drives and presynaptic inhibition of somatosensory feedback), locomotion is entirely defined by sensory feedback from the hindlimbs, operating in a state-machine regime.
evidence: This is a description of model behavior based on simulations.

claim: Removing supraspinal drives on one side to simulate a hemisection enhances the gains of somatosensory feedback and its dominant role in controlling the timing of the transition between the flexion and extension states of the ipsilesional RG.
source: Removing supraspinal drives on one side to simulate a hemisection enhances the gains of somatosensory feedback and its dominant role in controlling the timing of the transition between the flexion and extension states of the ipsilesional RG.
evidence: This is a description of model behavior based on simulations.

claim: In the hemisected model, the left contralesional circuits are mostly controlled by supraspinal drives, with the left RG mostly operating in a flexor-driven regime.
source: In the hemisected model shown in Figure 1B, the left and right spinal circuits still interact centrally as in the intact model, but the left contralesional circuits are mostly controlled by supraspinal drives, with the left RG mostly operating in a flexor-driven regime.
evidence: This is a description of model behavior based on the model architecture shown in Figure 1B.

claim: On the right ipsilesional side of the hemisected model, the circuits are mainly controlled by somatosensory feedback, with the right RG operating in a state-machine regime.
source: On the right ipsilesional side, the circuits are mainly controlled by somatosensory feedback, with the right RG operating in a state-machine regime.
evidence: This is a description of model behavior based on the model architecture.

claim: All parameters of the remaining pathways and neurons in the hemisected model were identical to the intact model parameters.
source: All parameters of the remaining pathways and neurons in the hemisected model were identical to the intact model parameters from Rybak et al., 2024.
evidence: This is a statement about the modeling methodology.

claim: The intact side of the hemisected model shows speed-dependent changes of cycle and phase durations that are almost identical to those of the intact model.
source: Based on this comparison, the following qualitative observations can be made for tied-belt locomotion. (1) The intact side of the hemisected model shows speed-dependent changes of cycle and phase durations that are almost identical to those of the intact model (Figure 2B1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2B1.

claim: The lesioned side shows an increase in flexor phase durations and a decrease of extensor phase durations relative to the intact state without changes in cycle durations.
source: (2) The lesioned side shows an increase in flexor phase durations and a decrease of extensor phase durations relative to the intact state without changes in cycle durations (Figure 2B2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2B2.

claim: Speed-dependent control of cycle and phase durations during locomotion on a split-belt treadmill significantly depends on whether the intact or lesioned limb is stepping on the slow or fast belt.
source: Speed-dependent control of cycle and phase durations during locomotion on a split-belt treadmill significantly depends on whether the intact or lesioned limb is stepping on the slow or fast belt (Lecomte et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: In the Left slow/Right fast condition, cycle and phase durations of the left contralesional (slow) side remained relatively constant with an increase of right belt speed.
source: With an increase of βR, cycle and phase durations of the left contralesional (slow) side remained relatively constant (Figure 3A1)
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3A1.

claim: In the Left slow/Right fast condition, on the right-hemisected (fast) side, a pronounced speed-dependent reduction of extensor phase durations compensated by a corresponding increase of flexor phase durations was observed.
source: whereas on the right-hemisected (fast) side, we observed a pronounced speed-dependent reduction of extensor phase durations compensated by a corresponding increase of flexor phase durations.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3A2.

claim: In the right ipsilesional hindlimb during Left slow/Right fast condition, stance and swing phase durations intersected at βR = 0.6-0.7 and the duty factor became less than 50% with further increase of βR.
source: In the right ipsilesional hindlimb, stance and swing phase durations intersected at βR = 0.6-0.7 and, with a further increase of βR, the duty factor became less than 50% (Figure 3A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3A2.

claim: In the Left slow/Right fast condition, on the left contralesional (slow) side, cycle and extensor phase durations are longer in comparison to the intact model without noticeable differences in flexor phase durations.
source: By comparing speed-dependent changes in cycle and phase durations obtained from the intact model in our previous simulations (Rybak et al., 2024, Fig. 6A), we can see that on the left contralesional (slow) side, cycle and extensor phase durations are longer in comparison to the intact model without noticeable differences in flexor phase durations (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the Left slow/Right fast condition, the most dramatic changes relative to the intact model were seen on the right-hemisected (fast) side where a significant speed-dependent reduction of extension and corresponding increase of flexion occurred with a duty factor falling below 50% in the middle of the speed interval.
source: The most dramatic changes relative to the intact model were seen on the right-hemisected (fast) side where a significant speed-dependent reduction of extension and corresponding increase of flexion occurred with a duty factor falling below 50% in the middle of the speed interval (Figure 3B2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3B2.

claim: In the Left fast/Right slow condition, cycle and phase durations on both sides do not change much with an increase of left belt speed.
source: In this case, cycle and phase durations on both sides do not change much with an increase of βL (cycle and extension durations slightly decrease on both sides and the flexion durations slightly increase on the intact side and slightly decrease on the hemisected side; Figure 4A1 and A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4A1 and A2.

claim: In the Left fast/Right slow condition, comparisons with the intact model show similar changes for both fast and slow sides.
source: Comparisons with the corresponding speed-dependent changes in cycle and phase durations in our intact model (Rybak et al., 2024, Fig. 6A) show similar changes for both fast and slow sides (Figure 4B1 and B2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results shown in Figure 4B1 and B2.

claim: Cycle and phase durations were recorded from nine cats before and after a mid-thoracic (T5-T6) lateral hemisection on the right side during tied-belt locomotion from 0.4 to 1.0 m/s.
source: We recorded cycle and phase durations of the left and right hindlimbs before and after a mid-thoracic (T5-T6) lateral hemisection on the right side in nine cats during tied-belt locomotion from 0.4 to 1.0 m/s
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology.

claim: Cycle and phase durations were recorded from eight cats during split-belt locomotion with the slow side stepping at 0.4 m/s and the fast side stepping from 0.5 m/s to 1.0 m/s.
source: and in eight cats during split-belt locomotion with the slow side stepping at 0.4 m/s and the fast side stepping from 0.5 m/s to 1.0 m/s.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology.

claim: Only cats that stepped up to 1.0 m/s during tied-belt (n = 5) and split-belt (n = 6) locomotion 7–8 weeks after hemisection were retained for analysis.
source: For this study, we only retained for analysis cats that stepped up to 1.0 m/s during tied-belt (n = 5) and split-belt (n = 6) locomotion 7–8 weeks after hemisection.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology and data selection criteria.

claim: During tied-belt locomotion, cycle duration significantly decreased with increasing speed in the left (p=1.81 × 10–12) and right (p=1.01 × 10–12) hindlimbs.
source: During tied-belt locomotion, cycle duration significantly decreased with increasing speed in the left (p=1.81 × 10–12) and right (p=1.01 × 10–12) hindlimbs
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: During tied-belt locomotion, there was no significant difference in cycle duration between the intact and hemisected states (p=0.074 and p=0.076 for the left and right hindlimbs, respectively).
source: with no significant difference between the intact (Figure 5A1 and A2) and hemisected (Figure 5B1 and B2) states (p=0.074 and p=0.076 for the left and right hindlimbs, respectively) (Figure 5C1 and C2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Stance phase durations significantly decreased with increasing speed for the left (p=1.07 × 10–17) and right (p=3.14 × 10–18) hindlimbs during tied-belt locomotion.
source: Stance phase durations also significantly decreased with increasing speed for the left (p=1.07 × 10–17) and right (p=3.14 × 10–18) hindlimbs.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Stance duration was noticeably longer after hemisection for the left contralesional hindlimb (p=0.045), but not for the right ipsilesional hindlimb (p=0.278) during tied-belt locomotion.
source: Stance duration was noticeably longer after hemisection for the left contralesional hindlimb (p=0.045), but not for the right ipsilesional hindlimb (p=0.278).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Swing duration significantly decreased with increasing speed after hemisection for the left contralesional hindlimb (p=0.011) and the right ipsilesional hindlimb (p=5.99 × 10–5) during tied-belt locomotion.
source: Swing duration significantly decreased with increasing speed after hemisection for the left contralesional hindlimb (p=0.011) and the right ipsilesional hindlimb (p=5.99 × 10–5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The hemisection had no significant effect on swing duration for the left contralesional hindlimb compared to intact (p=0.231) during tied-belt locomotion.
source: Overall, the hemisection had no significant effect on swing duration for the left contralesional hindlimb compared to intact (p=0.231, Figure 5C1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5C1.

claim: In the right ipsilesional hindlimb, swing duration across speeds became significantly longer after hemisection compared to intact (p=0.033) during tied-belt locomotion.
source: However, in the right ipsilesional hindlimb, swing duration across speeds became significantly longer after hemisection compared to intact (p=0.033, Figure 5C2).

claim: On the contralesional left side of hemisected cats, speed-dependent changes of cycle and phase durations were qualitatively similar to those of intact cats during tied-belt locomotion.

(1) On the contralesional left side of hemisected cats, speed-dependent changes of cycle and phase durations were qualitatively similar to those of intact cats.

claim: On the ipsilesional side of hemisected cats, cycle and phase durations changed considerably during tied-belt locomotion, particularly because of a large proportional increase of the swing phase duration.

claim: In contrast to simulations, the stance durations on the right ipsilesional side did not change following hemisection during tied-belt locomotion.
source: However, in contrast to our simulations, the stance durations on the right ipsilesional side did not change following hemisection.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with simulation results.

claim: During Left slow/Right fast split-belt locomotion, cycle duration slightly decreased with increasing right belt speed in the left (p=1.2 × 10–7) and right (p=1.87 × 10–7) hindlimbs.
source: Cycle duration slightly decreased with increasing right belt speed in the left (p=1.2 × 10–7) and right (p=1.87 × 10–7) hindlimbs.

claim: After hemisection, cycle duration across speeds was significantly greater compared to the intact state for the left (p=0.044) and right (p=0.046) hindlimbs during Left slow/Right fast split-belt locomotion.
source: After hemisection, cycle duration across speeds was significantly greater compared to the intact state for the left (p=0.044) and right (p=0.046) hindlimbs.

source: with no effect of the hemisection (p=0.066 and p=0.996 for the left and right hindlimbs, respectively).

evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Swing duration was significantly longer after hemisection in the right hindlimb (p=0.003) but not in the left hindlimb (p=0.985) during Left fast/Right slow split-belt locomotion.
source: Swing duration was significantly longer after hemisection in the right hindlimb (p=0.003) but not in the left hindlimb (p=0.985).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The experimental results generally confirm the modeling prediction that spinal hemisection does not change cycle and phase durations on both sides in comparison with intact cats when the ipsilesional hindlimb is stepping on the slow belt, other than a small increase of swing duration in the ipsilesional hindlimb.
source: The experimental results generally confirm our modeling predictions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) that spinal hemisection does not change cycle and phase durations on both sides in comparison with the corresponding characteristics in intact cats when the ipsilesional hindlimb is stepping on the slow belt, other than a small increase of swing duration in the ipsilesional hindlimb.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The hemisected model generated cycle and phase durations that qualitatively matched those obtained experimentally during tied-belt and split-belt locomotion.
source: Although our hemisected model is built on many simplifications, as discussed in detail in Rybak et al., 2024, it generated cycle and phase durations that qualitatively matched those obtained experimentally during tied-belt and split-belt locomotion.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation and experimental results throughout the manuscript.

claim: The model can reproduce experimental data in intact and spinal-transected animals.
source: This provides additional validation of our model as it can reproduce not only experimental data in intact and spinal-transected animals (Rybak et al., 2024)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the previous publication.

claim: The model makes predictions on expected changes in locomotor characteristics following an incomplete SCI without additional changes or adjustments of model parameters.
source: but also, without additional changes or adjustments of model parameters, it makes several predictions on expected changes in locomotor characteristics following an incomplete SCI.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling methodology described in the manuscript.

claim: The increase of ipsilesional swing duration is because of a greater influence of feedback from muscle afferents of right hip flexors (r-SF-E1) on the right flexor half-center due to the loss of presynaptic inhibition from supraspinal drive.
source: Based on our model (Figure 1), the increase of ipsilesional swing duration is because of a greater influence of feedback from muscle afferents of right hip flexors (r-SF-E1) on the right flexor half-center due to the loss of presynaptic inhibition from supraspinal drive.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on the model architecture shown in Figure 1.

claim: The increase in stance duration on the contralesional left side could be due to increased inhibition from the right flexor half-center via commissural interneurons.
source: The increase in stance duration on the contralesional left side, according to our model, could be due to increased inhibition from the right flexor half-center via commissural interneurons.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on the model architecture, presented as a possibility.

claim: Cats may use a voluntary strategy to shift weight support to the less affected hindlimb.
source: In cats, we cannot exclude that they can use a voluntary strategy to shift weight support to the less affected hindlimb.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible cat behavior.

claim: Greater load-related group Ib feedback (l-SF-E2 in the model) for the left slow limb in the Left slow/Right fast condition increases excitatory inputs to the left extensor half-center, prolonging left hindlimb stance duration.
source: Greater load-related group Ib feedback (l-SF-E2 in the model) for the left slow limb in the Left slow/Right fast condition increases excitatory inputs to the left extensor half- center, prolonging left hindlimb stance duration.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on the model architecture.

claim: In cats, a greater body shift toward the slow belt and greater extensor activity in muscles of the limb stepping on the slow belt is observed, consistent with greater group Ib feedback.
source: In cats, we observe a greater body shift toward the slow belt and greater extensor activity in muscles of the limb stepping on the slow belt, consistent with greater group Ib feedback (Frigon et al., 2015; Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental observations.

claim: Having the ipsilesional hindlimb stepping on the fast belt increased the asymmetry between hindlimbs compared to the intact state in the Left slow/Right fast split-belt condition.
source: What we observed, with both simulated and experimental results, is that having the ipsilesional hindlimb stepping on the fast belt increased the asymmetry between hindlimbs compared to the intact state, with longer swing and stance durations for the ipsilesional and contralesional hindlimbs, respectively, in the Left slow/Right fast split-belt condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by both simulation and experimental data.

claim: Having the ipsilesional hindlimb step on the slow belt in the Left fast/Right slow split-belt condition produced simulation and experimental results that were similar to the intact state.
source: However, having the ipsilesional hindlimb step on the slow belt in the Left fast/Right slow split-belt condition produced simulation and experimental results that were similar to the intact state.
evidence: This claim is supported by both simulation and experimental data.

claim: Having the ipsilesional hindlimb step on the slow belt forces it to increase its support as swing duration of the left contralesional hindlimb increases as left belt speed also increases.
source: We propose that it forces the ipsilesional hindlimb to increase its support as swing duration of the left contralesional hindlimb increases as left belt speed also increases.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observed results.

claim: The increase in support of the ipsilesional right hindlimb stepping on the slow belt increases the excitatory influence of r-SF-E2 or group Ib feedback on the right extensor half-center.
source: This increases the excitatory influence of r-SF-E2 or group Ib feedback on the right extensor half-center.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on the model architecture.

claim: Without the increase in support of the ipsilesional right hindlimb stepping on the slow belt, the animal could not perform split-belt locomotion.
source: Without this increase in the support of the ipsilesional right hindlimb stepping on the slow belt, the animal could not perform split-belt locomotion.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the necessity of the observed behavior.

claim: Prolonged use of split-belt locomotion for rehabilitation might be a way to reduce asymmetries following lateralized neurological injuries, such as SCIs and stroke.
source: From a clinical perspective, prolonged use of split-belt locomotion for rehabilitation might be a way to reduce asymmetries following lateralized neurological injuries, such as SCIs and stroke (Reisman et al., 2010; Reisman et al., 2013; Kuczynski et al., 2017; Lecomte et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative clinical application supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The model does not account for the interactions between the fore- and hindlimbs.
source: For instance, the model does not account for the interactions between the fore- and hindlimbs (Frigon, 2017; Harnie et al., 2024)
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the model.

claim: The model does not include properties of the musculoskeletal system and a pattern formation network that shape neural outputs.
source: and does not include properties of the musculoskeletal system and a pattern formation network that shape neural outputs (McCrea and Rybak, 2008; Markin et al., 2016; Frigon et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the model.

claim: The lack of possible plastic changes in spinal sensorimotor circuits of the model may explain the absence of exact/quantitative correspondences between simulated and experimental data.
source: The lack of possible plastic changes in spinal sensorimotor circuits of our model may explain the absence of exact/quantitative correspondences between simulated and experimental data.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for discrepancies between model and experimental results.

claim: It will be important to consider neuroplastic changes that occur over time following SCI in future computational studies designed to explain post-injury changes.
source: In future computational studies designed to explain post-injury changes, it will also be important to consider neuroplastic changes that occur over time following SCI, such as changes in neuronal excitability and the establishment of new neural pathways (Raineteau and Schwab, 2001; Bareyre et al., 2004; Murray et al., 2010; Rossignol and Frigon, 2011).
evidence: This is a recommendation for future work supported by citations to previous research on neuroplasticity.

claim: Simulated results were only compared to experimental results obtained 7–8 weeks after hemisection, when locomotor recovery was relatively robust.
source: In the present study, we only compared simulated results to experimental results obtained 7–8 weeks after hemisection, when locomotor recovery was relatively robust.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental methodology and timing.

claim: It is difficult to surgically perform a perfect lateral hemisection and some spinal tissue is often damaged on the contralateral side and/or spared on the ipsilesional side.
source: Experimentally, it is also difficult to surgically perform a perfect lateral hemisection and some spinal tissue is often damaged on the contralateral side and/or spared on the ipsilesional side.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental limitations based on practical experience.

claim: Striking similarities were observed between simulations and experimental studies despite some inconsistencies.
source: Nevertheless, although some characteristic changes predicted by the model were not fully consistent with our experimental results, we observed striking similarities between our simulations and the consequent experimental studies.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the overall agreement between model and experiment.

claim: Modeling sensorimotor interactions can be a powerful tool to predict and mechanistically explain changes following complete SCI, possibly serving as tool to guide rehabilitation efforts.
source: This indicates that modeling sensorimotor interactions can be a powerful tool to predict and mechanistically explain changes following complete SCI, possibly serving as tool to guide rehabilitation efforts.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the modeling approach based on the study results.

claim: To simulate a right lateral hemisection, all supraspinal drives from the right side were set to zero.
source: To simulate a right lateral hemisection, all supraspinal drives from the right side were set to zero, transforming the intact model (Figure 1A) to a hemisected model (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the modeling methodology.

claim: No other model parameters were changed to simulate hemisection.
source: No other model parameters were changed.
evidence: This is a statement about the modeling methodology.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the Animal Care Committee of the Université de Sherbrooke (Protocol 442-18) in accordance with policies and directives of the Canadian Council on Animal Care.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the Animal Care Committee of the Université de Sherbrooke (Protocol 442-18) in accordance with policies and directives of the Canadian Council on Animal Care.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the experiments.

claim: The current data set was obtained from nine adult purpose-bred cats (>1 year of age at the time of experimentation), five females and four males, weighing between 4.0 kg and 6.2 kg.
source: We obtained the current data set from nine adult purpose-bred cats (>1 year of age at the time of experimentation), five females and four males, weighing between 4.0 kg and 6.2 kg, purchased from Marshall BioResources (North Rose, NY).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: The ARRIVE guidelines 2.0 for animal studies were followed.
source: We followed the ARRIVE guidelines 2.0 for animal studies (Percie du Sert et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about adherence to reporting guidelines.

claim: Cats were used in other studies to investigate different scientific questions, some of which have been published.
source: In order to maximize the scientific output of each animal, they were used in other studies to investigate different scientific questions, some of which have been published (Lecomte et al., 2022; Merlet et al., 2022; Lecomte et al., 2023; Mari et al., 2023; Audet et al., 2023; Mari et al., 2024a; Mari et al., 2024b).
evidence: This is a statement about the use of animals in multiple studies, supported by citations.

claim: A lateral hemisection was performed between the fifth and sixth thoracic vertebrae (T5-T6) on the right side of the spinal cord after collecting data in the intact state.
source: After collecting data in the intact state, we performed a lateral hemisection between the fifth and sixth thoracic vertebrae (T5-T6) on the right side of the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a description of the surgical procedure.

claim: Paw contact was defined as the first frame where the paw made visible contact with the treadmill surface.
source: Paw contact was defined as the first frame where the paw made visible contact with the treadmill surface.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: Cycle duration was measured from successive paw contacts.
source: We measured cycle duration from successive paw contacts
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: Stance duration corresponded to the interval of time from foot contact to the most caudal displacement of the toe relative to the hip.
source: while stance duration corresponded to the interval of time from foot contact to the most caudal displacement of the toe relative to the hip (Halbertsma, 1983).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methodology supported by citation.

claim: Swing duration was calculated as cycle duration minus stance duration.
source: We calculated swing duration as cycle duration minus stance duration.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: Lesion extent estimations for individual cats after the right lateral hemisection ranged from 40.7% to 66.4% (50.3 ± 10.3%).
source: Lesion extent estimations for individual cats after the right lateral hemisection ranged from 40.7% to 66.4% (50.3 ± 10.3%) (Lecomte et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the lesion extent supported by citation.

claim: A two-factor (state × speed) repeated-measure ANOVA was performed for each dependent variable to determine the effect of locomotor state and speed on cycle, stance, and swing durations.
source: To determine the effect of locomotor state and speed on cycle, stance, and swing durations during quadrupedal tied- and split-belt locomotion, we performed a two-factor (state × speed) repeated-measure ANOVA for each dependent variable.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis methodology.

claim: Significance level was set at p<0.05.
source: Significance level was set at p<0.05.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical analysis methodology.
